screens.title: Neutron fundamentals: networks, subnets, routers
screens.narratorSegment: Neutron is OpenStack's networking service that exposes programmable network primitives to tenants. A network is an isolated Layer 2 segment; think of it as a virtual switch where instances connect and can see each other. A subnet defines the IP address range, gateway, and DNS servers inside that network; this is the addressing plan that instances will use. A router links networks and enables traffic to move between them; importantly, routers often need an external gateway mapped to a provider network to allow outbound traffic to the internet. For example, you create a private network for a tenant and then create a subnet with a 192.168.1.0/24 CIDR and a gateway address. You attach that subnet to a router, and set the router's gateway to an external provider network so instances can access external resources. A common misconception is to assume an instance with a tenant IP automatically has internet access; without a router with an external gateway, it cannot. Another mistake is overlapping CIDRs between subnets, which causes routing conflicts. Your role is to ensure address planning, gateway configuration, and clear mapping between virtual networks and any required physical mappings so tenants have predictable connectivity. After this, you'll apply these primitives with CLI examples and verification steps.

keyIdea.title: Neutron defined
keyIdea.text: Network = L2 segment, Subnet = IP addressing range and gateway, Router = connects networks and provides external gateway.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Neutron fundamentals
Definitions and roles
  • Network: an isolated Layer 2 segment where instances attach and communicate.
  • Subnet: an IP address range with gateway and DNS settings for that network.
  • Router: a logical device that connects networks and can be given an external gateway for outbound traffic.
Analogy
Think of a network as a building floor, a subnet as the room's wiring plan and addresses, and the router as the building's exit to the city.
Common mistake
Assuming instances have internet access without verifying the router's external gateway. Verify router configuration to avoid this issue.
Concrete example
# Create a private network
openstack network create private-net

# Create a subnet in that network
openstack subnet create --network private-net \
  --subnet-range 192.168.1.0/24 \
  --gateway 192.168.1.1 \
  --dns-nameserver 8.8.8.8 \
  private-subnet

# Create a router and attach the subnet
openstack router create my-router
openstack router add subnet my-router private-subnet

# Set the router gateway to an external provider network
openstack router set --external-gateway external-net my-router
Key Takeaway

Define addressing and gateway intentionally; verify router external gateway to provide external connectivity.

screens.title: Create a tenant network, subnet, and router
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through the exact process of creating a tenant private network, adding a subnet, creating a router, and connecting the router to an external provider network. Start by creating the network and subnet to define the Layer 2 domain and the addressing plan. Use a non-overlapping CIDR like 10.0.0.0/24 for tenant networks to avoid conflicts with other projects. After creating the subnet, create a router and add the subnet to it; this enables routing for instances on that subnet. The crucial final step is setting the router's external gateway to a provider network; without this the router cannot forward traffic to external networks. Verify each step with list and show commands: listing networks, subnets, and routers ensures resources exist; inspect the router's external_gateway_info to confirm gateway configuration. A common mistake is choosing an incorrect gateway address or forgetting to map the router to the provider network. Also check security group and floating IP assignment policies if instances still cannot reach the internet. After you run the flow you should be able to trace packets from an instance's tenant IP to the external network via the router and gateway. Reflect: if an instance cannot reach the internet, which verification command will you run first?

keyIdea.text: Create network → create subnet with CIDR → create router → attach subnet → set router external gateway; verify with list and show commands.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Create Tenant Network
Step-by-step
  1. Create the private network for the project and confirm creation.
  2. Create a subnet with a CIDR, gateway, and DNS entries; avoid overlapping ranges.
  3. Create a router and add the subnet so the tenant has routed connectivity.
  4. Set the router's external gateway to a provider network for outbound access.
  5. Verify with network, subnet, and router list/show commands.
Verification checklist
Run: openstack network list; openstack subnet list; openstack router show <router> and inspect external_gateway_info.
CLI Example
# Create a new private network
openstack network create tenant-private-net

# Create a subnet in the private network
openstack subnet create --network tenant-private-net \
  --subnet-range 10.0.0.0/24 \
  --gateway 10.0.0.1 \
  --dns-nameserver 8.8.8.8 \
  tenant-private-subnet

# Create a router and attach the subnet
openstack router create tenant-router
openstack router add subnet tenant-router tenant-private-subnet

# Set the router's gateway to the external network
openstack router set --external-gateway external-net tenant-router
Key Takeaway

Follow address planning and verify gateway configuration to ensure outbound connectivity for tenant instances.

screens.title: Provider networks vs Project (self-service) networks
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between provider networks and project networks is essential when designing cloud network topology. A provider network is directly mapped to physical network infrastructure and typically used for external connectivity or when instances need direct access to the physical network for performance or hardware-based features. Provider networks are simpler and high-performance, but they give tenants less flexibility because they rely on fixed physical mappings. Project networks, sometimes called self-service networks, are virtual and isolated for each tenant. They commonly use overlays such as VXLAN or VLAN to encapsulate traffic across the shared physical fabric, enabling multi-tenancy and flexible topologies without changing the physical network. In practice you will choose provider networks for floating IPs or high-bandwidth services and project networks when you want tenants to create complex internal topologies without affecting other tenants. A frequent error is exposing tenant networks to physical networks without proper security controls or misconfiguring the external gateway so that tenants cannot reach the internet. When planning, weigh performance needs against the benefits of isolation and tenant autonomy. Reflection: which workloads in your environment need direct physical access versus isolated virtual networks?

keyIdea.title: Network choice
keyIdea.text: Provider networks = physical mapping and performance; Project networks = virtual isolation, overlays, and tenant flexibility.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Provider vs Project Networks
Provider Networks
  • Mapped to physical networks for direct connectivity and high performance.
  • Used for floating IPs, external access, or services requiring physical network features.
  • Simpler mapping but less tenant-level flexibility.
Use case example: public-facing web tier that needs predictable bandwidth and low latency.
Project (Self-Service) Networks
  • Virtual, tenant-owned networks using overlays like VXLAN or VLANs.
  • Provide strong isolation and flexible topologies without changing physical switches.
  • Great for multi-tenancy and self-service networking.
Use case example: tenant staging environments that require full virtual network control without touching the physical fabric.
Trade-off
Performance and simplicity versus flexibility and isolation.
Common mistake
Exposing project networks directly to physical networks or misassigning external gateways, causing security or connectivity issues.
Pro Tip
Document which services require provider networks and reserve those physical mappings to prevent accidental tenant exposure.

screens.title: Neutron CLI examples and verification
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson focuses on the CLI commands you'll use frequently to create and verify Neutron resources. The commands are simple but each step must be verified. First, create a network and subnet with the expected CIDR and DNS settings. Then create a router and add the subnet. Finally, set the router's external gateway to the provider network. After each change, use listing and show commands to confirm the resource exists and is configured as expected. For example, create a private network, then the subnet with a 192.168.1.0/24 range and assign a gateway and DNS. Create a router, add subnet to it, and set the router's gateway. When connectivity fails, inspect the router with a show command and look for external_gateway_info. A misconception to avoid is thinking the network interface inside the instance guarantees outbound access; the router and external gateway must be in place. Use the openstack network list, subnet list, and router list commands to ensure the resources are created, and router show to verify gateway details. Practice these commands until verification becomes a routine step in your deployment process.

Create resources (example)

openstack network create private-net

# Create a subnet in that network
openstack subnet create --network private-net \
  --subnet-range 192.168.1.0/24 \

  • Use openstack router list and openstack router show <router> to inspect external_gateway_info.
  • If connectivity fails, confirm CIDRs do not overlap and that floating IPs are available on the provider network.
Misconception: instance IP equals internet access. Confirm the router has an external gateway first.

screens.title: Cinder block storage: volumes and persistence
screens.narratorSegment: Cinder is OpenStack's Block Storage service that supplies persistent block devices to virtual machines. A Cinder volume behaves like a physical hard drive presented to an instance; it survives instance termination unless explicitly deleted. This persistence makes volumes suitable for databases, stateful applications, or any workload that needs durable storage beyond the life of a VM. Volume lifecycle operations include create, attach, detach, snapshot, and delete. A snapshot captures the state of a volume at a point in time, enabling backups or cloning workflows. For example, create a 10GB volume and attach it to an instance; if you later terminate the instance, the volume remains and can be attached to another instance. A common misconception is that volumes automatically back up to object storage; snapshots are separate operations and must be created intentionally. Another operational point: use volume types to reflect backend capabilities like SSD or HDD and offer tiered storage to users. Practically, you'll monitor volumes and snapshots and ensure policies for retention and deletion to manage capacity. Consider access patterns: is the workload read-heavy, write-heavy, or latency-sensitive? That informs volume type selection.

keyIdea.title: Volume behavior
keyIdea.text: Cinder volumes are persistent block devices that remain after instance termination unless deleted; snapshots capture their state for cloning or backup.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Cinder volumes
What is a Cinder volume?
  • Persistent block storage exposed to instances like a regular disk.
  • Volumes persist independently from instance lifecycle unless deleted.
  • Snapshots capture a volume state and can be used to create new volumes.
Example: create a 10GB volume and attach it to a running instance to hold database files that outlive the VM.
Operational notes

Use snapshots for backups or to create derived volumes. Choose volume types to map to backend characteristics and enforce policies for retention and deletion to avoid capacity issues.

Common mistake
Assuming snapshotting is automatic. Snapshots must be created and managed as part of your backup plan.
Key Takeaway

Treat volumes as durable resources; plan volume types and snapshot cadence based on workload requirements.

screens.title: Volume types and tiered storage with Cinder
screens.narratorSegment: Volume types let administrators expose different storage backends and performance characteristics to users while maintaining a simple A P I. For example, you might create a "high-performance-ssd" volume type backed by an SSD-enabled Ceph pool, and an "archive-hdd" volume type backed by spinning disks for cold data. When users request a volume and specify a volume type, Cinder provisions the volume from the matching backend. This enables tiered storage: workloads with strict input and output requirements get SSD-backed volumes, while infrequently accessed data uses lower-cost HDD pools. Designing volume types requires coordination with storage teams to ensure pools are created, properly sized, and have appropriate replication settings. A misconception is that volume types automatically migrate data between backends; they only control new provisioning. You must plan migration or re-provisioning strategies if data needs to move between tiers. Finally, document volume type names, backend mappings, and quotas so tenants can request the correct tier for their workload's performance and cost profile. This approach keeps operations predictable while offering flexibility to users. Volume types and tiered storage with Cinder means volume types map provisioning requests to specific backends, enabling administrators to offer storage tiers like ssd or hdd transparently to users.. In practical terms, mapping volume types to backends for performance tiers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Volume Types & Tiering
Why volume types matter

Volume types create an abstraction layer so users request capacity without knowing backend details. Admins map volume types to storage pools or backends to enforce performance, replication, and capacity characteristics.

  • Create named volume types such as high-performance-ssd and archive-hdd.
  • Map types to Ceph pools or other Cinder backends.
  • Use quota and policy controls to manage usage across tiers.
Concrete example
Define two volume types: one backed by an SSD Ceph pool for latency-sensitive databases, and another backed by HDD pools for archival data. Users request the type at volume creation to receive the appropriate storage characteristics.
Misconception: volume types move existing data automatically between tiers. They only control provisioning for new volumes.
Operational tip
Coordinate with Ceph or storage admins to create pools with appropriate replication and performance settings before mapping volume types.
Documentation
Keep a clear mapping of volume type name → backend pool for support and billing purposes.
Key Takeaway
Volume types are the mechanism for offering tiered storage and aligning user requests with backend capabilities.

screens.title: Cinder CLI: create volumes and snapshots
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through the typical Cinder CLI interactions: creating a volume, creating a snapshot, and provisioning a new volume from a snapshot. Creating a volume is straightforward and requires a size and name; snapshots capture the volume state for cloning or backup. When creating a volume from a snapshot you supply the snapshot identifier and a size equal to or larger than the snapshot's source volume. After creating the snapshot, verify it appears in the snapshot list and is in the available state before using it to create a new volume. A common pitfall is failing to wait until the snapshot operation completes; attempting to create a volume from an in-progress snapshot will fail. Also verify backend pool capacity before creating many snapshots or large volumes. Use volume attach operations to expose the block device to an instance and then perform in-guest filesystem operations as usual. Finally, practice detaching and cleaning up volumes in a lab to avoid orphaned storage. These steps form a routine backup-and-clone workflow for stateful applications. Cinder CLI: create volumes and snapshots means create volumes → snapshot volume → create new volume from snapshot; verify states between steps and confirm backend capacity.. In practical terms, practical commands and verification for snapshots and cloning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Cinder CLI
Common commands
# Create a 10GB block storage volume
openstack volume create --size 10 my-data-volume

# Create a snapshot of a volume
openstack volume snapshot create --volume my-data-volume my-data-volume-snapshot

# Create a new volume from a snapshot
openstack volume create --snapshot my-data-volume-snapshot --size 10 new-volume-from-snapshot
Verification and cautions
  • Confirm the snapshot status becomes available before creating a volume from it.
  • Verify backend capacity to avoid provisioning failures.
  • Plan retention for snapshots to avoid unexpected storage consumption.
Exercise: create a snapshot, wait for it to become available, then provision a new volume from it and attach to a test instance to validate integrity.
Key Takeaway

Snapshots enable cloning and backups, but always verify completion and pool capacity before provisioning derived volumes.

screens.title: Red Hat Ceph Storage: role and advantages
screens.narratorSegment: Red Hat Ceph Storage is a software-defined storage platform that provides unified block, object, and file services. When integrated with OpenStack, Ceph's RBD (RADOS Block Device) is commonly used as the Cinder backend to provide replicated, scalable block volumes. Ceph offers fault tolerance through data replication across OSDs, scalability by adding more storage nodes, and unified access for images and objects as well as block devices. For Cinder this means volumes can be highly available and performant when Ceph is properly sized and networked. Key considerations include the number of OSDs, placement group sizing, and separating public and cluster networks to avoid network contention. Common mistakes are under-provisioning Ceph resources or misconfiguring pools, both of which can lead to performance bottlenecks or reduced availability. Regularly monitoring Ceph health is essential; use the Ceph CLI to check cluster status and pool listings. In designs, plan replication and failure domains to meet your tolerance for data loss and recovery speed. Ceph gives OpenStack the resilient backend that many production clouds require. Red Hat Ceph Storage: role and advantages means ceph provides replicated, scalable rbd storage for cinder, delivering resilience and unified storage services when sized and networked correctly.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Ceph integration
What Ceph provides
  • RBD for block volumes with replication and distribution across OSDs.
  • Scalability by adding OSDs and storage nodes.
  • Unified backend for Cinder volumes and Glance images.
Design points: plan OSD counts, placement groups, and separate public/cluster networks for best performance.
Operational concerns

Under-provisioned OSDs or incorrectly sized placement groups lead to performance bottlenecks. Misconfigured pools can affect availability. Monitor cluster health to detect issues early.

Common mistake
Failing to separate traffic between public and cluster networks, which can degrade performance under load.
Key Takeaway

Ceph provides RBD-backed volumes for Cinder with strong resilience and scalability when designed and monitored carefully.

screens.title: Ceph operational checks and commands
screens.narratorSegment: Regularly checking Ceph cluster health and pool settings is a critical operational activity. The two most common commands are to check overall cluster status and to list pools so you can confirm expected pools exist for Cinder and Glance. When a cluster reports HEALTH_OK you can be confident replication and OSDs are functioning; HEALTH_WARN or HEALTH_ERR require investigation. Inspecting pool lists helps you validate that pools used by volume types or image backends are present. If pools are missing or misconfigured, Cinder provisioning can fail or use the wrong pool semantics, impacting performance or availability. A common mistake is not monitoring placement group distribution and OSD usage, which leads to hotspots and degraded performance. Use ceph status regularly in maintenance scripts and alerting, and query ceph osd pool ls when validating deployment. Keep watch for degraded placement groups, down OSDs, and utilization spikes. These checks let you act before users experience data loss or slow input and output. Ceph operational checks and commands means use ceph status and ceph osd pool ls to validate cluster health and pool presence; respond quickly to warn or err states.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Ceph Checks
Health and pools
# Check Ceph cluster status (if integrated)
sudo ceph status

# List Ceph pools
sudo ceph osd pool ls
Interpretation: HEALTH_OK is expected; any WARN/ERR requires investigation into OSDs, PGs, or network issues.
Operational guidance

Schedule regular Ceph checks and integrate them into monitoring and alerts. Validate that Cinder-related pools exist and have appropriate replication and size settings.

Common mistake: ignoring PG distribution and OSD usage until performance degrades; proactively monitor these metrics.
Key Takeaway

Run Ceph status and pool checks frequently and respond to warnings to maintain storage reliability and performance.

screens.title: Guided lab: create tenant network, router, and Cinder volume
screens.narratorSegment: This guided lab ties together the networking and storage workflows covered so far. During the lab, watch for common issues like overlapping CIDRs or a missing external gateway. The lab also recommends practicing detaching the volume and deleting it safely to avoid orphaned storage. Use these steps to build confidence in provisioning and verification before applying changes to production. keyIdea.text: Provision tenant network and router, set external gateway, create and snapshot a volume, and verify every resource with list/show commands.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Guided Lab
Networking steps (follow and verify)
# Assume 'external-net' exists or create a placeholder
# openstack network create --external --provider-physical-network datacentre --provider-network-type flat external-net

# Create a new private network
openstack network create tenant-private-net

# Create a subnet in the private network
openstack subnet create --network tenant-private-net \
  --subnet-range 10.0.0.0/24 \
  --gateway 10.0.0.1 \
  --dns-nameserver 8.8.8.8 \
  tenant-private-subnet

# Create a router
openstack router create tenant-router

# Connect the private subnet to the router
openstack router add subnet tenant-router tenant-private-subnet

# Set the router's gateway to the external network
openstack router set --external-gateway external-net tenant-router
Storage steps (create and snapshot)
# Create a 10GB block storage volume
openstack volume create --size 10 my-data-volume

# (Attach to an instance as needed using your environment's attach method)
# Create a snapshot of the volume
openstack volume snapshot create --volume my-data-volume my-data-volume-snapshot

# Create a new volume from the snapshot
openstack volume create --snapshot my-data-volume-snapshot --size 10 new-volume-from-snapshot

# Verification commands
openstack network list
openstack subnet list
openstack router list
openstack router show tenant-router
openstack volume list
openstack volume snapshot list
Lab checkpoint
Confirm router external_gateway_info and that the snapshot status is available before creating a derived volume.
Safety tip
Detach and delete volumes carefully in lab environments to avoid orphaned storage. Use your cloud's recommended detach workflow.
Key Takeaway
Follow verification steps after each operation to catch configuration mistakes early.

screens.title: Troubleshooting common networking and storage failures
screens.narratorSegment: When connectivity or storage issues occur, systematic troubleshooting saves time. For networking problems start by checking that the instance has an IP from the expected subnet, then confirm the router exists and that its external_gateway_info is set. If the router lacks a gateway, set it and re-test connectivity; the most likely missing configuration for a tenant instance that cannot reach the internet is the router's external gateway. Also check for overlapping CIDRs or incorrect gateway addresses which block routing. For storage problems, verify that volumes are in the available or in-use states and that snapshots are complete before cloning. If provisioning fails, inspect the backend storage for capacity or pool misconfiguration. For Ceph-backed storage, run cluster health checks to identify down OSDs, degraded placement groups, or pool absence. A common operational pitfall is under-provisioning Ceph OSDs or forgetting to separate public and cluster networks, which leads to contention and slow input and output. Use the verification commands we've covered as your first step, and then escalate to backend logs and Ceph health details when necessary. Always document the symptom, the verification results, and the corrective actions you took.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Troubleshooting
Networking checks
  • Confirm the instance IP is in the correct subnet and that security group rules allow egress.
  • Run router show and inspect external_gateway_info for the gateway mapping.
  • Check for overlapping CIDRs or incorrect gateway configuration that blocks routing.
Storage checks
  • Ensure the volume is in the expected state (available or in-use) and snapshots are complete.
  • If using Ceph, run ceph status and inspect pools and OSD health for degraded PGs or down OSDs.
  • Validate pool configuration and capacity to prevent provisioning failures.
Documentation
Record verification outputs and steps taken so teams can reproduce fixes and prevent recurrence.
Escalation
If backend checks show Ceph WARN/ERR, escalate to storage operations with Ceph status outputs and affected pool names.
Key Takeaway
Start with simple verification; then inspect router gateways and Ceph health to find root causes of connectivity or storage issues.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Networking & Storage
screens.narratorSegment: These three key concepts summarize the chapter. First, Neutron provides networks, subnets, and routers—networks are Layer 2 domains, subnets define IP ranges and gateways, and routers connect networks and require an external gateway for internet access. Second, Cinder offers persistent block volumes and snapshots; volumes persist beyond instance lifetimes and volume types enable tiered storage for different performance needs. Third, Red Hat Ceph Storage is a robust backend for Cinder via RBD: it offers replication, scalability, and unified storage but must be sized and networked correctly and monitored regularly. Keep these concepts in mind during design and troubleshooting: verify router gateway settings for connectivity issues, choose appropriate volume types for workload performance, and monitor Ceph health to prevent data availability issues. These are the operational anchors you will return to when designing, deploying, and maintaining an OpenStack cloud.

screens.title: Three Practical Reminders
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three practical rules at hand. One: always verify router external_gateway_info when instances lack external access — this is the most common missing configuration. Two: use volume types to map user requests to appropriate backends; this simplifies cost control and performance guarantees. Three: integrate Ceph health checks into your monitoring; respond to HEALTH_WARN or HEALTH_ERR to prevent wider storage impact. Apply these rules in routine checks and automation. For example, include router show and openstack network list in your deployment smoke tests, have named volume types for SSD and HDD tiers in your service catalog, and schedule ceph status checks with automated alerts. These simple practices reduce mean time to repair and make day-to-day operations predictable. As you operate RHOSP at scale, these reminders will help you detect misconfigurations early and choose the right storage tier for each workload.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the practical essentials of Neutron networking and Cinder block storage, plus how Red Hat Ceph Storage integrates as a backend. We'll cover how tenants define networks, subnets, and routers, the difference between provider networks and project networks, and the commands you will use to create these resources. You will also learn how Cinder provides persistent block volumes, how volume types enable tiered storage, and why Ceph's RADOS Block Device is a common production choice. This matters because virtual machines need predictable connectivity and durable storage; misconfigured routers or under-provisioned storage backends are common failures in production clouds. As an RHCA you will design network topologies, map provider networks to physical infrastructure, choose appropriate volume types, and size Ceph clusters for reliability. A brief concrete example: create a private project network, attach a subnet and router, then set the router gateway to an external provider network so instances can reach the internet. Throughout we'll show commands and verification steps so you can reproduce these actions in a real environment. Think about a recent outage: was it network segmentation or a storage misconfiguration? That question frames what we solve here.

By the end of this chapter you will configure tenant networks, define subnets and routers, and ensure external connectivity using provider networks. You will also create and manage persistent block storage with Cinder, including creating snapshots and choosing suitable volume types for workload requirements. Finally, you will understand how Red Hat Ceph Storage integrates with Cinder and Glance, why RBD is used for block volumes, and what production considerations—like OSD counts and network separation—matter for performance and resilience. Each objective focuses on hands-on verification and common pitfalls: for example, confirming a router's external gateway or monitoring Ceph health. A concrete example: after creating a tenant network and router you will verify external access using router inspection commands and network listings. These skills matter because they let you design multi-tenant, resilient clouds and respond faster when connectivity or storage issues arise. You will leave able to adopt volume types for tiered storage and to read Ceph status outputs to detect under-provisioning or pool misconfiguration.

This second objectives page emphasizes applied skills and lab readiness. You will practice CLI workflows to create tenant networks, subnets, and routers, then verify the router's external gateway so instances can reach the internet. For storage, you'll create a 10GB Cinder volume, attach it to an instance, and create a snapshot to preserve state. You will also learn to choose and configure volume types to present tiered storage options to users. Finally, you will perform Ceph health checks, list pools, and learn which misconfigurations commonly cause degraded performance or availability. A concrete lab example: use the provided network and volume commands to set up a tenant environment, then confirm with list and show commands. The emphasis is on verification: running router show, network list, and Ceph status. These verification steps help you find whether a missing external gateway or an under-provisioned Ceph pool is the root cause of an outage. This screen prepares you for the guided lab that follows.

Neutron is OpenStack's networking service that exposes programmable network primitives to tenants. A network is an isolated Layer 2 segment; think of it as a virtual switch where instances connect and can see each other. A subnet defines the IP address range, gateway, and DNS servers inside that network; this is the addressing plan that instances will use. A router links networks and enables traffic to move between them; importantly, routers often need an external gateway mapped to a provider network to allow outbound traffic to the internet. For example, you create a private network for a tenant and then create a subnet with a 192.168.1.0/24 CIDR and a gateway address. You attach that subnet to a router, and set the router's gateway to an external provider network so instances can access external resources. A common misconception is to assume an instance with a tenant IP automatically has internet access; without a router with an external gateway, it cannot. Another mistake is overlapping CIDRs between subnets, which causes routing conflicts. Your role is to ensure address planning, gateway configuration, and clear mapping between virtual networks and any required physical mappings so tenants have predictable connectivity. After this, you'll apply these primitives with CLI examples and verification steps.

This screen walks through the exact process of creating a tenant private network, adding a subnet, creating a router, and connecting the router to an external provider network. Start by creating the network and subnet to define the Layer 2 domain and the addressing plan. Use a non-overlapping CIDR like 10.0.0.0/24 for tenant networks to avoid conflicts with other projects. After creating the subnet, create a router and add the subnet to it; this enables routing for instances on that subnet. The crucial final step is setting the router's external gateway to a provider network; without this the router cannot forward traffic to external networks. Verify each step with list and show commands: listing networks, subnets, and routers ensures resources exist; inspect the router's external_gateway_info to confirm gateway configuration. A common mistake is choosing an incorrect gateway address or forgetting to map the router to the provider network. Also check security group and floating IP assignment policies if instances still cannot reach the internet. After you run the flow you should be able to trace packets from an instance's tenant IP to the external network via the router and gateway. Reflect: if an instance cannot reach the internet, which verification command will you run first?

Understanding the difference between provider networks and project networks is essential when designing cloud network topology. A provider network is directly mapped to physical network infrastructure and typically used for external connectivity or when instances need direct access to the physical network for performance or hardware-based features. Provider networks are simpler and high-performance, but they give tenants less flexibility because they rely on fixed physical mappings. Project networks, sometimes called self-service networks, are virtual and isolated for each tenant. They commonly use overlays such as VXLAN or VLAN to encapsulate traffic across the shared physical fabric, enabling multi-tenancy and flexible topologies without changing the physical network. In practice you will choose provider networks for floating IPs or high-bandwidth services and project networks when you want tenants to create complex internal topologies without affecting other tenants. A frequent error is exposing tenant networks to physical networks without proper security controls or misconfiguring the external gateway so that tenants cannot reach the internet. When planning, weigh performance needs against the benefits of isolation and tenant autonomy. Reflection: which workloads in your environment need direct physical access versus isolated virtual networks?

This lesson focuses on the CLI commands you'll use frequently to create and verify Neutron resources. The commands are simple but each step must be verified. First, create a network and subnet with the expected CIDR and DNS settings. Then create a router and add the subnet. Finally, set the router's external gateway to the provider network. After each change, use listing and show commands to confirm the resource exists and is configured as expected. For example, create a private network, then the subnet with a 192.168.1.0/24 range and assign a gateway and DNS. Create a router, add subnet to it, and set the router's gateway. When connectivity fails, inspect the router with a show command and look for external_gateway_info. A misconception to avoid is thinking the network interface inside the instance guarantees outbound access; the router and external gateway must be in place. Use the openstack network list, subnet list, and router list commands to ensure the resources are created, and router show to verify gateway details. Practice these commands until verification becomes a routine step in your deployment process.

Cinder is OpenStack's Block Storage service that supplies persistent block devices to virtual machines. A Cinder volume behaves like a physical hard drive presented to an instance; it survives instance termination unless explicitly deleted. This persistence makes volumes suitable for databases, stateful applications, or any workload that needs durable storage beyond the life of a VM. Volume lifecycle operations include create, attach, detach, snapshot, and delete. A snapshot captures the state of a volume at a point in time, enabling backups or cloning workflows. When connectivity or storage issues occur, systematic troubleshooting saves time. For networking problems start by checking that the instance has an IP from the expected subnet, then confirm the router exists and that its external_gateway_info is set. If the router lacks a gateway, set it and re-test connectivity; the most likely missing configuration for a tenant instance that cannot reach the internet is the router's external gateway. Also check for overlapping CIDRs or incorrect gateway addresses which block routing. For storage problems, verify that volumes are in the available or in-use states and that snapshots are complete before cloning. If provisioning fails, inspect the backend storage for capacity or pool misconfiguration. For Ceph-backed storage, run cluster health checks to identify down OSDs, degraded placement groups, or pool absence. A common operational pitfall is under-provisioning Ceph OSDs or forgetting to separate public and cluster networks, which leads to contention and slow input and output. These three key concepts summarize the chapter. First, Neutron provides networks, subnets, and routers—networks are Layer 2 domains, subnets define IP ranges and gateways, and routers connect networks and require an external gateway for internet access. Second, Cinder offers persistent block volumes and snapshots; volumes persist beyond instance lifetimes and volume types enable tiered storage for different performance needs. Third, Red Hat Ceph Storage is a robust backend for Cinder via RBD: it offers replication, scalability, and unified storage but must be sized and networked correctly and monitored regularly. Keep these concepts in mind during design and troubleshooting: verify router gateway settings for connectivity issues, choose appropriate volume types for workload performance, and monitor Ceph health to prevent data availability issues.
